utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good morning. Your Honours, today the Prosecution will respond to General Mladic's motion requesting that this Chamber enter a judgement of acquittal on all counts of the indictment on the grounds that there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. General Mladic's motion must be denied in its entirety. The Prosecution has tendered and the Chamber has admitted the evidence of over 360 witnesses and approximately 5.200 exhibits. This corpus of evidence establishes clearly and unequivocally each of the crimes enumerated in the indictment, the role General Mladic played in those crimes, and his criminal liability for them. Before we review our evidence, it may be useful to first briefly set out our understanding of Mr. Ivetic's submissions yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You're kindly asked to slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: First, Mr. Ivetic has requested that the Chamber depart from the well-established legal test applied to a 98 bis motion. I will address that in a few moments. Second, the Defence challenges the Prosecution's proof with respect to the overarching joint criminal enterprise set out in the indictment. I will also address the Chamber on this. It is our understanding of the Defence motion that it makes a very limited challenge to Counts 9 and 10 of the indictment related to Sarajevo. Ms. Bibles will address the Chamber on this challenge to scheduled crime G1. The Defence challenges specific allegations related to the municipalities component of the case and including Schedule D as well as some specific allegations and individual crimes listed in Schedules A and B. Mr. Traldi will address those arguments. Mr. McCloskey will address several challenges to the Srebrenica component of the case. The Defence challenges Prosecution proof with respect to crimes in which non-members of the VRS took part or played a primary part. Both Mr. Traldi and Mr. McCloskey will address those aspects of the argument. Ms. Bibles will address the Chamber on challenges related to Counts 1 and 2 of the indictment, the crime of genocide. And I will conclude our submissions by addressing the Chamber on Mr. Ivetic's broad challenge to our proof establishing liability pursuant to 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. The Defence has made a submission that the Prosecution will not address in its response. Defence raised a number of issues related to how the indictment was pled. Rule 72 applies to such applications, and in this case the Chamber has already received and already decided upon the Defence Rule 72 application. Let me first address the jurisprudence. Mr. Ivetic spent a considerable amount of time during his submissions encouraging the Chamber to abandon well-established jurisprudence governing the test to be applied to General Mladic's Rule 98 bis application. In sum, he suggests that this Chamber should depart from this jurisprudence and examine the proof related to specific factual allegations and specific incidents, and where it finds proof lacking dismiss that particular allegation from the indictment. The analysis and test that the Trial Chamber must apply has been recently restated by the Appeals Chamber in its 98 bis judgement in the Karadzic case. It summered the test in paragraph 21 of its judgement, which I will now read: "The Appeals Chamber recalls that a judgement of acquittal shall only be entered pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Rules 'if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction.' The test to be applied by the Trial Chamber is 'whether there is evidence, if accepted, upon which a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused on the particular charge in question.' Pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Rules, a Trial Chamber is required to 'assume that the Prosecution's evidence is entitled to credence unless incapable of belief' and to take the evidence at its highest. It cannot 'pick and choose among parts of that evidence' in reaching its conclusion." In the context of General Mladic's motion, the jurisprudence is clear, that should the Chamber find there is sufficient evidence which, if credited, could establish General Mladic's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt for a particular count of the indictment, the motion must be denied with respect to that count. This standard has been applied consistently since the plenary of Judges adopted the current version of Rule 98 bis in 2004. This test was applied in deciding the 98 bis motions made by Mrksic, Martic, Milutinovic and his co-accused, Prlic and his co-accused, Milan Lukic and his co-accused, and most recently in the Hadzic case. Should this Chamber departing from this for the last 98 bis application before this Tribunal? The simple answer is no. Mr. Ivetic has set out no reason for this Chamber to apply a different test. The Prosecution has prepared its submissions today with the expectation that the Chamber will apply this established standard. Should the Chamber be inclined to adopt the standard proposed by Mr. Ivetic, I submit that procedural fairness requires that we know that and be given an opportunity to prepare our submissions accordingly. Finally, I would conclude my introductory remarks by saying the Defence submissions, for the most part, have focused on narrow aspects of individual counts with the exception of their broad attack on evidence establishing Mladic's 7(1) and 7(3) liability as well as genocide. Their submissions leave much of the Prosecution's case uncontested with respect to individual counts. The Defence, by tailoring its arguments to a legal standard that does not exist, has failed in many respects to demonstrate that there is a basis for granting the relief sought under Rule 98 bis. Yesterday at transcript 20768, the Defence suggested that insufficient evidence had been adduced to support the charge that General Mladic shared or intended to further the common purpose of the overarching JCE. In fact, the evidence clearly demonstrates that between 12 May 1992 and 30 November 1995, General Mladic was a pivotal figure in the evolution and the execution of an overarching criminal plan. The aim of this plan, whose genesis was in October of 1991, was the forcible and permanent removal of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the Bosnian Serb claimed territory. Put simply, the aim was ethnic cleansing. This plan was to be achieved through the commission of the crimes including deportation, inhumane acts, murder, extermination, and persecutions as charged in Counts 3 to 8. The campaign of persecutions would in some municipalities escalate to include the crime of genocide. Yesterday the Defence argued that the Prosecution failed to establish Mladic's liability for genocide under JCE III. Conflating concepts of both intent and liability, Mr. Ivetic, once again, urges the Chamber to ignore what he, himself, called "established case law before this Tribunal" and reject JCE III convictions for specific intent crimes. As recently as January of this year, the Djordjevic Appeals Chamber affirmed that an accused can be found criminally liable under the third category of joint criminal enterprise for specific intent crimes, provided that the crimes were reasonably foreseeable to the accused. When Mladic joined the overarching JCE to rid Bosnian Serb territories of non-Serbs, it was foreseeable to him that genocide was a possible consequence of implementation of the common plan. This common plan of the JCE was conceived of and implemented by the leading Bosnian Serb and Serbian political, military, and police figures. It was a plan that was overarching, of three additional and related JCEs. The crimes committed pursuant to and in furtherance of these JCEs ultimately furthered this overarching plan. The terror created through the campaign of shelling and sniping in Sarajevo, Counts 9 and 10, was used to exert pressure on the international community and the Bosnian government in order to achieve their demographic objectives. The taking of UN personnel hostage, Count 11, was aimed at gaining leverage over the UN and NATO for the same purpose. The forcible transfer and murder operations in Srebrenica were the starkest, most audacious examples of this persecutory campaign. The most prominent participants in the overarching JCE and these other three related JCEs were President Karadzic, president of the presidency and later the expanded presidency of the Republika Srpska and the supreme commander of its armed forces; and General Mladic, the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Though Mr. Ivetic claimed that "the mere position General Mladic held within the VRS cannot be used as primary evidence to infer his criminal responsibility," the Prosecution has never relied on Mladic's formal role as its strongest evidence of his culpability. Mladic contributed to the common purpose of the overarching JCE primarily through his authority and his ability to engage the armed forces under his command in the commission of crimes. Mladic also oversaw the VRS's co-operation with other institutions linked to other members of the JCE and who were similarly engaged in furtherance of the overarching plan. These includes the RS Crisis Staffs, War Presidencies, and the Bosnian Serb police under the control of President Karadzic. For example, see the evidence of RM097 and adjudicated facts 363 and 365, as well as 373 and 405. Through JCE liability, Mladic is responsible for such crimes committed by these entities regardless of whether they were committed by forces directly subordinated to the VRS or other institutions linked to members of the JCE. This co-operation between JCE structures is shown by the patterns and the systemic nature of the crimes committed and some of the discussions held between JCE members, including meetings of the RS presidency, the Supreme Command, and the RS Assembly. And I would refer to Reynaud Theunens expert report, P3029, which discuss such meetings in detail. The existence of this common plan and General Mladic's involvement in it is demonstrated by the patterns of the crimes committed during the take-over operations that began in April 1992 and the operations that followed General Mladic's appointment as commander of the VRS. Other indications of this plan include the six strategic objectives when considered in their context and the military directives, orders, and instructions issued pursuant to and in furtherance of the strategic objectives. The circumstances in which the strategic objectives were formulated and in which General Mladic was appointed can be understood from a number of entries in his military notebook, P352. These reflect discussions in the week before Mladic's appointment, discussions held with key JCE members Karadzic and Krajisnik. Together, these entries tell a story that places a persecutory campaign at the heart of the VRS' war objectives. On the 5th of May, 1992, Mladic recorded a discussion concerning the objectives of the VRS and the "relationship towards non-Serbian inhabitants in the territory"; that is P352 of e-court page 246. At this time the relationship toward non-Serb inhabitants was characterised by expressions of leading JCE members in favour of ethnic separation. For example, during March 1992 both Karadzic and Krajisnik made speeches at Bosnian Serb assembly sessions in which they advocated ethnic division and contemplated take-overs of Serb claimed territory; in particular, Zvornik. These are noted in the expert report of Robert Donja, P2001. A few weeks later, BBC journalist Martin Bell witnessed 20.000 Muslim refugees outside the town of Zvornik, following an attack by JCE member Zeljko Raznatovic, aka Arkan; that's P832. In a 6th of May entry, Mladic noted that "in Bratunac, two representatives of the SDS are killing all Muslims by slitting their throats"; this is P352 at page 253. He also records Karadzic stating: "It would be a disaster if we did not separate with them"; that's P352 at page 257. In the context of these violent take-overs on the 7th of May, during a closed meeting of select people, the strategic objectives were set out by Krajisnik and noted down by Mladic in his notebook. Karadzic was also present at this meeting. The first of the strategic objectives as noted by Mladic in his notebook states: "1. To separate from the Croats and Muslims forever"; that's page 262. Karadzic and Krajisnik were looking for an accomplished military commander capable of carrying out the type of persecutory campaign that had already begun.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. The first of these strategic objectives noted down by Mladic states: "To separate from the Croats and Muslims forever." Karadzic and Krajisnik were looking for an accomplished military commander capable of carrying out the type of persecutory campaign that they had already begun, someone with a proven track record, someone who would consolidate gains made since April 1992 and continue the process of seizing Serb claimed territory. Mladic had demonstrated his credentials for such a task while a commander in the JNA 9th Corps in Croatia during the autumn of 1991. There, soldiers under his command comitted crimes against non-Serbs in Serb claimed territories. This pattern of seizing territory and forcibly removing civilians in areas in Croatia would be repeated in Bosnia, as observed in the Krajisnik testimony of Milan Babic, now an exhibit in the case, and the expert report of Reynaud Theunens. On the 12th of May, 1992, Mladic attended the 16th Assembly Session. At the end of that session, the VRS was formally established and General Mladic was formally installed as the commander of the VRS Main Staff. At that session, President Karadzic outlined the six strategic objectives to the plenary, stating: "The first such goal is separation from the other two national communities, separation of states." The remaining five objectives set out by the Bosnian Serb leadership identified their geographic aspirations, territory which had been or would be seized, dominated, and ethnically cleansed. These objectives were articulated in the context of an ongoing campaign of ethnic cleansing. Following their promulgation and Mladic's appointment as commander of the VRS, this campaign increased in its scope and its scale. It is this context and the widespread pattern and systematic nature of the related criminal operations that give the strategic objectives their criminal implications. Within days of his appointment --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was talking about what happened immediately after the promulgation of the six strategic objectives, and it was in this context that the widespread pattern and systemic nature of the related criminal operations that gives the strategic objectives their criminal implications. Within days of his appointment, the VRS, under General Mladic's direction, began contributing to the implementation of the overarching criminal plan. The first charge crime, Schedule A6.2, took place in Hambarine on the 23rd of May, 1992, and by mid-June massacres had been perpetrated by his soldiers in six different municipalities. One way in which Karadzic and Mladic applied the forces under their command was by turning the strategic goals into operational directives. As P338, at page 159 indicates, this is the 1993 VRS combat readiness report. This demonstrates that the strategic goals served as a "general guide-line" for the VRS. This evidence is directly contrary to Mr. Ivetic's submission yesterday that Mladic somehow disagreed with the strategic objectives. JCE members met to discuss the progress made in implementing the strategic objectives. Following such meetings, operational directives would be issued implementing orders passed down the chain of command and military operations carried out. Some of these operations included the commission of serious crimes. The meetings prior and the events following the issuance of Directives 4 and 7 are notable examples of the way in which the political goal of permanent ethnic separation became absorbed into regular army orders which led to the commission of crimes. Yesterday the Defence argued that the evidence shows General Mladic did not share intent related to any common purpose that has been identified by the Prosecution. This was at transcript page 20772. The crimes committed in furtherance of the JCE were clearly intended by Mladic and his fellow JCE members. Throughout our submissions here today, we will be referring to evidence of this shared intent. The evidence establishes the General Mladic created, shaped, and led the VRS to perpetrate the crimes contemplated by the overarching JCE. The claims made yesterday by the Defence that there was a frail connection between General Mladic and the acts for which he now stands trial is simply not credible. There is a very clear connection between General Mladic and the crimes committed in pursuance of the overarching JCE. Through skillful and effective use of command and control principles, such as single command, subordination, inspection, he established a system through which his orders flowed efficiently down the chain of command and the information he needed rapidly back up. That gave him what expert General Dannatt described as "finger-tip control" over the soldiers under his command. His full and active engagement with his troops in the field ensured that he was often present at the most critical events in the war, such was his commitment that on occasion his forcefulness and precision would rise to the level of micromanaging particular campaigns. Lest there be any confusion, Mladic's finger-tip control, his ability to engage his forces with precision, is as important to any assessment of his criminal liability under Article 7(1) of the Statute as it is under Article 7(3). His ability to effectively command VRS soldiers and apply them in the commission of crimes was his primary contribution to the joint criminal enterprise as set out in paragraph 13 of the indictment. I would ask you to keep this in mind as we review the evidence of the crimes and how they were committed. As my colleagues will describe, he used this control to devastating effect in his efforts to conquer and cleanse Serb claimed territory. I will now ask Mr. Traldi to respond to the Defence arguments related to the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning. General Mladic and the VRS, in co-operation with forces under the control of other JCE members, implemented the common criminal purpose Mr. Groome described in a brutally efficient genocidal and persecutory campaign throughout the Bosnian municipalities. That campaign is charged in Counts 1 and 3 through 8 of the indictment. In addressing the Defence arguments about these counts, I will start with the objectives of that campaign, turn to Mladic's role in implementing it, and finally deal with the campaign itself. It is necessary to understand this was a single campaign in which each crime contextualises and explains each other crime. I will thus address the criminal nature of the campaign and not artificially segregate specific incidents. General Mladic himself described the Bosnian Serbs' territorial objectives and demonstrated that he fundamentally shared in the common criminal purpose of the JCE. You can see on what should be the next slide, C2, that these targeted areas spanned the length and width of Bosnia. In an interview in evidence as P1975, General Mladic called for taking "back the territory Muslims took during World War II and as punishment, even more than that," and he called for achieving "the unification of the Serbian lands from Knin, through Banja Luka and Sarajevo, to Belgrade." And if you look at the blue areas on the map, you can see what General Mladic meant. Knin is just to the west and Croatia, and then the blue areas extend through the ARK, the Posavina corridor, cover the entire eastern border regions, and include the areas of Sarajevo claimed by the Bosnian Serb leadership. These areas parallel the territory identified by strategic objectives 2 through 6. These were the territories which Bosnian Serb leaders told Witness Okun they intended to make "ethnically pure Serb or as overwhelmingly Bosnian Serb as they could make it." And that's in P3103, page 23. I'd refer you also to P431, page 49. General Mladic knew that this was a massive undertaking. Slide C3 shows that he told the RS Assembly: "People and peoples are not pawns nor are they keys in one's pocket that can be shifted from here to there. It is something easily said but difficult to achieve." The way that the JCE achieved what Mladic termed "shifting people and peoples from here to there" was an organised campaign of ethnic cleansing through co-ordinated military operations in municipality after municipality. Other crimes, including the destruction of cultural heritage sites and the large scale detention of non-Serb civilians, were committed to facilitate this ethnic cleansing process. Slide C4 shows that General Mladic cogently expressed the JCE member's common purpose to the RS Assembly in 1994, describing their historic chance to create a "all Serbian state," and "all Serbian" didn't leave much room for the people who lived in Ahatovici or Brdo or Zepa. And you can see on slide C5 how similarly other Bosnian Serb authorities described their common purpose. The first quote is particularly instructive in showing how the permanent nature of the forcible removal of non-Serbs flowed directly from the Bosnian Serb leadership's policies. After Radovan Karadzic presented the strategic objectives, one assembly delegate, Miroslav Vjestica, rose and proudly noted that there were no more Muslims in Bosanska Krupa. Then he asked: "Will they have a place to return to?" And he answered: "I think it is unlikely after our president told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una is the border." And for your reference, Your Honours, P3853, page 9, shows that in 1995 Krupa was 100 per cent Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The emphasis on permanent separation, which Mladic recorded in his notebook on 5 May 1992 was an integral part of the campaign he was asked to implement. And as you see here, that emphasis lasted throughout the war. I'd refer you generally to Exhibits P2798 and P3072 regarding how Mladic and the other JCE members redrew the demographic map of Bosnia. General Mladic had an integral role in redrawing that map. He immediately established command and unified Bosnian Serb forces, and as commander of the Main Staff his orders -- his orders drove the JCE forwards. Mladic continually received information about how those orders were being carried out. This information is reflected in the trial record in four primary ways: First, his own notebooks in which he recorded many of his day-to-day meetings; second, the daily combat reports he received regularly from subordinate VRS corps; third, his participation in meetings with international observers; and fourth, records of other meetings he attended including meetings of the Republika Srpska government and meetings with local civilian authorities and lower level VRS officers. The record shows that the reports he received paralleled the testimony of many survivor witnesses. These reports describe different VRS brigades utilising the same tactics, committing the same crimes, and achieving the same criminal end. That consistency is not a coincidence. It is the inevitable result of decisions made at the strategic level to separate the population through the commission of crimes. Slide C6 shows a selection of the reports General Mladic received on the implementation of the JCE. The Defence asserted yesterday that Mladic did not know or have reason to know that crimes were being committed during this campaign. In fact, he was extensively informed about its criminal nature. His subordinate corps often reported on the removal of non-Serbs from Serb claimed territories. Several of the reports shown on this slide in the first section coincide with large ethnic cleansing operations in late May and late July. Indeed, VRS officers sometimes complained that civilian authorities were not efficient enough in removing non-Serbs from their municipalities, reporting, for instance, that the civilian authorities were not "sufficiently organised in implementing this model for removal of the enemy," or suggesting that they "work much harder at this." And that's P3815 and P3714. Other reports in General Mladic's notebooks described the flight of non-Serbs from Bratunac, Foca, Kalinovik, Kljuc, Zvornik, and Serb claimed areas around Sarajevo. Reports to General Mladic described the detention of large numbers of non-Serbs. And reports to General Mladic described murders which were repeated throughout the VRS campaign in the municipalities. From municipality to municipality, witnesses told the same story of the patterns of destruction wrought by Bosnian Serb forces: Serb take-overs of power; attacks against defenceless people or violence that continued long after the fighting had stopped; destruction of Bosnian Muslims' and Croats' towns and sacred places; detention of civilians as well as fighters in camps in inhumane conditions; organised expulsions to a few holdout enclaves; and large massacres, from Prijedor in the west to Vlasenica in the east, Foca in the south, and everywhere in between. These repeated patterns of crimes by forces under JCE members' control are highly relevant to showing their common purpose. I will focus on two for the moment. First, the killings across these municipalities reached a massive scale. P2796 and 2797 identify by name nearly 2.000 of the victims of the massacres charged in Schedules A and B of the indictment. These massacres, of course, led up to the killing of thousands more Bosnian Muslim men and boys when Srebrenica fell in July of 1995. Second, the Defence referred yesterday to the destruction of non-Serb cultural heritage sites. The only reasonable inference from the uniform destruction of these sites is that it was part of the JCE members' common purpose and their persecutory and genocidal campaign. Mr. Riedlmayer testified at transcript page 17933: No mosque in the indictment municipalities survived the war undamaged. This removed the core of non-Serb communities and the clearest visual evidence of their existence. The pattern of these destructions shows the widespread and systemic nature of the attack on non-Serb communities. The Defence asserted yesterday at transcript page 20743 that the Chamber cannot review evidence about uncharged cultural heritage sites. This is incorrect. Those sites are also relevant to prove the widespread and systemic nature of this campaign. And I'd refer Your Honours to paragraphs 746 and 766 of the Tolimir trial judgement regarding the relevance of these destructions to the perpetrator's mens rea. P4333, pages 89 and 90, reflects that the destruction of non-Serb sites was part of JCE members' policy. That's the evidence of Bosnian Serb official Predrag Radic. And it is clear from the evidence of one VRS soldier that the uniform destruction of mosques was part of the policy. When he was asked if there were 19 mosques in his municipality, he said there couldn't have been because if there had been, he and the other soldiers would have destroyed 19 mosques. That's at transcript page 17298. And I'd refer you also to Witness Taci's evidence, particularly at transcript page 2098. Several Bosnian Serb witnesses gave evidence which demonstrates how the destruction of mosques fit into the plan to permanently and forcibly remove non-Serbs. Your Honours have received evidence from Milan Tupajic, RM15, RM16, and RM513 that the Serbs believed that if the mosques were destroyed, the Muslims would not return. That's P3170, P2362, P1054, and transcript page 17388. The permanent change in the Bosnian landscape wrought by these destructions was precisely the point. As to the specific Defence arguments about individual sites, there is evidence in the trial record to support each charged site. Much of this is in Mr. Riedlmayer's evidence, particularly P2503, 2510, 2511, and 2514.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. While the Defence attempts to impugn some of Mr. Riedlmayer's sources, his conclusions are corroborated by pre- and post-damage photographs, witnesses evidence in this trial, and they are also corroborated in large part by facts adjudicated by the Chamber. Looking at the municipalities the Defence singled out yesterday, each site in Bijeljina is addressed in Mr. Riedlmayer's written evidence. P1054, paragraphs 77 and 78, discusses the large-scale destruction of mosques in Bijeljina by VRS forces and the message it sent, that non-Serbs should leave the area. P4163 shows the destruction of mosques in Bijeljina continued in 1993. And the Chamber has recognised the destruction of Bijeljina mosques in adjudicated fact 517. Each site in Pale is also addressed in Mr. Riedlmayer's written evidence, and Witness Crncalo testified at transcript page 3238 that all the mosques in Pale were destroyed while it was under SDS control. And perhaps my speed was off, but it was Witness Crncalo and transcript page 3238. Finally, Mr. Riedlmayer was unable to reach an expert conclusion that two of the four charged mosques in Kalinovik were destroyed during the indictment period, as the Defence pointed out. However, the Chamber has received witness evidence and found adjudicated facts on the subject. Indeed, as Mr. Ivetic pointed out, the Prosecution redacted P2800 on the basis of those facts. This evidence satisfies the Rule 98 bis standard even if the Chamber were to consider each mosque separately. The Defence also offered boilerplate challenges to a large number of Schedule A and B incidents in the span of a few sentences. To be fair to the other components, rather than go through each incident in detail, I will simply discuss the genocidal campaign and explain how those incidents fit into the implementation of the JCE members' common criminal purpose. We will provide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could I just ask you one question. You referred to a witness who testified in paragraph 77 and 78. It was -- what was it? It was 45. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's P1054. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, P105 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- it's evidence under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you refer to paragraph 77 and 78. Now, if I understood Mr. Ivetic well, it's not that he ignores the existence of this evidence but the issue he raised is that it is the quality of that evidence. I think he said when the witness explains how the mosques were destroyed that this information was spoken about in Bijeljina or, in paragraph 78, this was a clear signal to non-Serbs. And what he challenged is not the existence of that evidence but is that the witness apparently does not explain why he had the opinion that this was a clear signal, whether that is opinion or whether that is a statement of facts, and similarly for the sources of his information in paragraph 77. So if you say, Well, there is the evidence, then that seems not to respond to what Mr. Ivetic brought to our attention yesterday, if I understood you well, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd just make two brief responses, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: First, that looking at the quality of that evidence is precisely the type of weighing exercise that is for final judgement rather than for the 98 bis stage of this proceedings. Second, you singled out the quality of the witness' evidence, that this was a clear signal to non-Serbs that they should leave. As I mentioned a moment ago, that's evidence that the Chamber has also received from a number of other Bosnian Serbs witnesses, and I'd suggest, for corroboration and explanation, that those references are more than sufficient to provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's not only this quote from this witness but it is the broader picture which puts this into context. Is that how we have to understand your argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd say you've encapsulated it better than I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's not make it a competition. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'm also looking at the clock. We are far beyond the time we usually take a break. Perhaps I was a bit disturbed by the interruption we had halfway, although that was certainly less than the 15 minutes we are over time now. Since I have interrupted you, anyhow, Mr. Traldi, would it be of any problem if we would take the break now or would you finish a few sentences before we take the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, I was about to turn to a different topic and so this would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We take a break, and in view of the fact that we were a bit longer, perhaps we should take a slightly longer break and we resume at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Traldi, I would like to briefly address what may be not a significant issue. Mr. Groome, you commenced this morning your submissions by saying that the Prosecution will respond to General Mladic's motion requesting that this Chamber enter a judgement of acquittal on all counts of the indictment on the grounds that there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. Now, the Chamber is not aware of any motion. The Chamber is aware of the Defence having announced and asked for an opportunity to make submissions so as to assist the Chamber in fulfilling its duties under Rule 98 bis. Then later on you said that many of the counts had been left uncontested. Again, but perhaps I'm also addressing you, Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber understands the situation as that the Defence wanted to make submissions so that the Chamber could fulfil its duties under Rule 98 bis, and in that context made specific submissions on charges or counts in the way you did in which, I think, you enumerated in four specific items, of course, leaving the duties of the Chamber under Rule 98 bis in respect of any other matter still in existence. Is that how we have to understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You are correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, is it clear now or -- Rule 98 bis doesn't speak about the motion, and there is no motion before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having clarified this matter, Mr. Traldi is invited to continue his presentation of argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was about to turn to the JCE members's campaign. General Mladic's integral role is most visible in that campaign's rapid escalation after he formally assumed the post of commander of the VRS Main Staff. You can see on slide C7 a 1st Krajina Corps document from 21 May 1992 noting his appointment and the establishment of unified command, and in this excerpt noting the need to "struggle for complete separation from the Muslim and Croatian peoples." Within days the VRS was conducting large-scale operations throughout Bosnia. A senior VRS officer testified that cleansing territory on ethnic grounds was a regular feature of those operations. That's at T5012, 5013. The criminal nature of these operations is evident from Bosnian Serb documents. You can see the RS MUP's report of the killing or wounding of hundreds of inhabitants of non-Serb villages in Prijedor on slide C8. These attacks are charged as incidents A6.1 through 6.3. The Defence suggested yesterday that the Prosecution had not specifically identified the perpetrators. Instead, this is one of many instances where the crimes were committed in the context of a large-scale operation under VRS command by joint Serb forces subordinated to their local commander, then their corps commander, and then, of course, to General Mladic. Regarding operations in Prijedor at this time, I refer you also to P2243 and 2875. Other municipalities saw similar cleansing operations. P2889 and 3294, for instance, describe operations in Sanski Most. And while the Defence challenged the identity of the perpetrators of two other scheduled incidents in Drum and Kenjari around this time, in each case the Chamber received evidence that the perpetrators included soldiers in uniform. I'd refer Your Honours to P2489 and 3391. Slide C9 shows how these operations were carried out on the other side of Bosnia. Major Andric ordered expulsions of women and children from the Birac area in an organised and co-ordinated way and that all the men had to be kept in camps for exchange. You can see this applied in, for instance, P3737, P524, P4004, and P3170, page 46. Back in the ARK, P3872 shows a similar policy to what we see here. And P3599 and P3600 show the thousands deported to Croatia in the campaign's implementation. A summary of some of the key evidence about the campaign in late May and early June is on slide C10. Bosnian Serb authorities completed these operations by expelling most women and children and confining them, whether or not they were armed or fighters, in detention facilities in terrible conditions. Reports to Mladic around this time reflected significant numbers of prisoners, including women and children held all around the country: The ARK, Rajlovac, Ilidza, Susica. All of those are facilities where we've shown large-scale crimes were committed. The creation of detention facilities accelerated after the operations in late May because the VRS had taken so many non-Serbs prisoner. As you can see on slide C11, Batkovic camp, for instance, was created at General Mladic's order. I would refer you also to P189 and P377. Serious crimes were committed at Batkovic, several prisoners killed. At T9355, one Bosnian Serb witness called the camp a disgrace. Yesterday, the Defence asserted that the evidence was not sufficiently specific as to perpetrators of crimes at Batkovic. Of course, again, the commander remained in the VRS chain of command, subordinated to the East Bosnian Corps and to Mladic, and the guards subordinated to him. Indeed, all of the camps charged in the indictment fell within either the military or police chains of command, directly subordinated to members of the JCE. One example from around this time illustrates how the military and police co-operated in committing crimes in these facilities. In early June, shortly after the operations in the ARK, a delegation of high-ranking 1 KK officers, including General Talic, visited their new camp at Manjaca. They could see blood on the prisoners' faces and on their clothing. The 1st Krajina Corps then co-ordinated with the Sanski Most Crisis Staff to transfer from Sanski Most to Manjaca politicians, extremists, and those unwelcome in the municipality. That's T3001 and P2409 and 3255. And P2362 shows those unwelcome in the municipality meant basically all non-Serbs. In that transfer, at least six people were killed. This incident, B1.1, is another for which the Defence suggested yesterday the VRS bore no responsibility. Instead, it compelling illustrates the co-operation between JCE forces in committing crimes related to the detention camps. The next slide, C12, shows a selection of witness evidence, that detention of non-Serbs was done arbitrarily, on a large scale, by the VRS and served as a tool in forcibly removing non-Serbs. The Bosnian Serb authorities described their policy similarly. Slide C13 shows Minister Stanisic reporting to President Karadzic that the VRS was to arrest as many Muslim civilians as possible, many had been placed in camps with poor conditions run by the MUP. I'd refer Your Honours also to P3874. The Defence stated yesterday that certain camps involved RS MUP perpetrators. As reflected here, of course, that's true and has always been part of our case. The camp system illustrates how these different JCE members and their forces co-operated in implementing their common criminal purpose. While Minister Stanisic refers in this document to camps run by the MUP, detainees in camps run by the VRS were primarily civilians as well. P221 is a Manjaca camp report from July 1992 just days after this document, and it states clearly what Manjaca was, a camp for segregation of Muslims and Croats, which history will not forgive us. In early June 1992, Witness Wilson had challenged Mladic and RS presidency member Plavsic about the massive detention of non-Serb civilians. That's at T3997. But it continued throughout the war. I'd refer you to, for instance, P355, page 63; P2886; P3808; and P4008. This next slide shows the interrelated nature of the camp system. For instance, General Mladic could task multiple camps in the same order through his chain of command as he did in P201 and P2879. This map labels the detention facilities charged in Schedules B and C. The solid blue lines show areas where people were transferred from one municipality to another, to move them to or from one of the camps where General Mladic is charged with crimes. You can see the large number of dotted lines representing transfers between charged camps and the large number of lines pointing to the centres at Manjaca in the north-west and Kula near Sarajevo. Of course, dozens of other camps pockmarked the landscape of Bosnia. And on the left side of the map you can see what P2225 shows, that one witness was held in seven different detention facilities in the Sarajevo area during the summer of 1992, including Kula prison. That's only possible because the camps were a single co-ordinated system. Why hold tens of thousands of civilians in camps? Because they were part of implementing the permanent forcible removal of non-Serbs. You can see on the next slide, C15, green lines showing releases into either Croatian or Muslim held territory in Bosnia. For instance, when Manjaca was closed at the Main Staff's order, the VRS deported some detainees to Croatia. You can see that green line on the left side of the map. Other detainees were sent to other camps in the Bosnian Serb system and hidden from the international community. While many non-Serbs were held in camps, operations to ethnically cleanse remaining villages continued through the summer and fall. I'd refer you to P520 regarding Kljuc and P2440 regarding Prijedor. Yesterday, the Defence suggested that the Prosecution had not specifically identified the perpetrators of crimes committed during these operations. Those relate to Prijedor A6.5 through A6.9 inclusive, and Kljuc, A3.3. Again, these were co-ordinated operations under clear VRS command. For Prijedor, I'd refer you also to P2365, P2432, and transcript pages 17805 through 17807 among others. The Prijedor operations are particularly illustrative. An officer from the 6th Brigade told RM095 that the Muslim areas of Brdo and Biscani would be cleansed even though the population had surrendered their weapons. Non-Serbs from those areas were then massacred in a number of different villages. Others were brought to Keraterm and Omarska where hundreds more were killed. And the group that collected the bodies of the non-Serbs who had been killed in just one of these areas, Biscani, had to make 19 separate stops to pick up dead bodies. The campaign continued to devastate the Bosnian Muslim and Croat communities with massacres throughout the summer and fall. And I'll just briefly refer to one with which Your Honours are very familiar, evidence regarding the massacre at the Grabovica school. I refer to it because it illustrates like those operations much about the persecutory campaign. General Mladic had been personally involved in negotiations regarding the surrender of Vecici, the War Presidency had followed his instructions, that's in P2884, and then his forces, VRS forces, captured fleeing Muslims, took them to the school, and massacred at least 150 prisoners. This next slide, C16, shows the massacre was reported up the chain of command to the Main Staff and that the next day the 1st Krajina Corps reported that the same prisoners had been killed in combat, same number of persons. No VRS soldiers were ever punished and almost all of the victims' bodies are still missing. Having cleansing most of the areas they claimed, the JCE members then turned their focus to the remaining enclaves in the Drina Valley. Regarding the state of the campaign at this point, I'd ref you to Exhibits P320 and P2813. General Mladic issued an order creating the Drina Corps, P3659. Huge parts of the area it would cover had already been ethnically cleansed, and now the JCE members had a new VRS corps to finish the job. It would include brigades under Rajko Kusic and Svetozar Andric. Krstic's 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade became part of it soon afterwards. Each had already been responsible for serious crimes. On 8 November after the massacre at Grabovica, Mladic met with his corps commanders and JCE members Karadzic and Krajisnik. Slide C17 reflects some of his notes of that meeting. Here, Mladic records that Krajisnik noted: "We have achieved the corridor and separation with the Muslims," and then summarised "the most important objective is the task assigned to the Zivanovic," who, evidence shows, was the commander of the Drina Corps, "the mopping up of the Drina. The most important task is separation from the Muslims." Days later, Mladic signed Directive 4, P1968. It called for driving the enemy army out of the Drina Valley with the Muslim civilian population. And the Drina Corps issued an implementing order which was equally clear, and it read, in pertinent part: Force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde. And that's P2095. Many of the people in these enclaves had already been driven out of their homes and during this campaign many were re-expelled to Srebrenica. Witness Osmanovic summaries it eloquently on slide C20. His family -- C18 now, I'm sorry, I've done a little bit of cutting during the break. His family is just one of many which was driven from hamlet to hamlet or camp to camp by the implementation of the JCE. The Main Staff and its representatives were directly involved in cleansing this area, and on 15 February 1993 the Main Staff issued an attack order, P2218, which noted the enclaves had "the burden of a large number of civilian refugees," and used the ethnic slur "poturice." Villages in the targeted area were destroyed and burned. I want to turn to one last massacre to which the Defence referred to yesterday at length, the massacre at Skrljevita, charged at A7.5. The Defence told you yesterday that military police arrested the perpetrators, but failed to mention that VRS and SDS officials intervened to have those perpetrators released. That's at P2362, 2371, and 2375. And it's clear from P3294 that one was a former paramilitary who had been incorporated into the VRS. Contrary to some of the Defence arguments, far from wanting to stop this paramilitary from committing further crimes, VRS and SDS officials intervened to protect him from punishment when he was part of the murder of a group of unarmed Bosnian Croats. This incident is certainly relevant to the Chamber's assessment of the incorporation of paramilitaries. Indeed, as the VRS consolidated control over its targeted areas and expelled their non-Serbian populations, many of the commanders whose units committed the worst crimes in the municipalities were promoted through the ranks. This last slide, C19, shows some examples. Several of the same perpetrators committed more crimes under General Mladic's command later in the war, like Krstic and Kusic. Taking this campaign as a whole, the evidence of the crimes in the municipalities is clear, reliable, and overwhelming. A comprehensive review of each incident would require much more time. However, the evidence I have discussed, even in this limited time, is amply sufficient for the Chamber to dismiss the challenges to incidents addressed in Counts 1 and 3 through 8. Accordingly, I'll ask Mr. McCloskey to discuss the evidence showing how Mladic led the genocide at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are moving ahead a bit too quickly. It's still the morning, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I can't quite get the clock from here. It's not my purpose today to go over an exhaustive account of the -- Mladic's involvement in the Srebrenica genocide. You've heard that evidence and we all saw you listen very carefully with plenty of questions. I will refer you to my opening statement where I do identify some of the key links in our basic theory of our case, as well as our trial brief where we identify some of the key evidence. What I do want to do here in the some roughly 40 minutes that I have is respond to Mr. Ivetic's sometimes specific challenges. Now, as you saw most of his challenges had to do with the weight of the evidence or the credibility which, as we know, is not really what this kind of a challenge is about, but I will want to respond to it to give you a better context of how to look at some of this material. I want to start off with his challenge to Directive 7. He suggested in his comments that Mladic was somehow separate from Directive 7, and he stated -- Mr. Ivetic stated that, and I quote: "The corps commanders should not have reacted to Karadzic's directive before receiving Mladic's orders as a result of the directive." This is absolutely wrong. General Mladic and his Main Staff don't have the time nor energy and ability, as you've learned from the documents themselves and from the description of the experts, to lay out the details of combat plans. This is left to his corps. And we see this from the documents when we look at, for example, Krivaja 95. This is an operation by the Drina Corps that's approved be the Main Staff. It's not the other way around. So the Drina Corps is not waiting to develop a combat plan based on Directive 7. Of course we understand the reason why Mr. Ivetic wants to separate Mladic from Directive 7 because of its two now famous and criminal aspects. I won't go over that. You've heard it probably a hundred times. The first: Create an unbearable situation of total insecurity of the inhabitants of Srebrenica, one; two, the creation of unobtrusive system of permits to make the population dependent on their good will. It's important to understand just how involved General Mladic is. And I want you to actually -- I'm not going to show you many documents, but I do want you to see the front. P1469. This is Directive 7 and this should be -- a cover letter should come up that, you may recall, was in the name sent out from the chief of staff to the Main Staff, General Milovanovic. Now, here it is. General Milovanovic, who you've learned is the one person who can issue orders aside from Mladic, is on this document sending out Directive 7 and he wants the corps to confirm receipt of the above mentioned directive by returning a copy of this document. Now, I think you understand at this point that when General Milovanovic sends out a document from the Main Staff to his corps they understand this is a very serious order. And General Mladic is just a big part of this as General Milovanovic and President Karadzic who actually signed the order. Go back to the testimony of the chief of operations, Obradovic and others, explain to us how directives are made. They are made at the Main Staff by the serious -- the sectors, the expert sectors, be they morale, legal, religious, security, operations, logistics, all those staffs get together and they create this document and it's put together by the chief of operations and training, Directive 7, in this case General Miletic. You'll recall that his name is the person that drafted it. So this is a Main Staff document, created by the Main Staff, sent to President Karadzic who reviews it, signs it, as we see it gets sent back to the Main Staff, the Main Staff sends it out. And you'll remember the words of Directive 7: "By well organised, planned and organised combat operations, create an unbearable situation ..." So Mladic is every bit a part of this directive as Karadzic and Miletic. Now the language, we may never know who put in that famous criminal language. Did Karadzic put it in or did Mladic put it? It sounds very similar to the chief of the Bratunac Brigade's report in July 4th 1994, P1505 that also talks about creating an unbearable situation. But, Your Honours, it's important to understand who wrote it does not matter. They both own this. There is no dual chain of command problem. Karadzic is the Supreme Commander as we know; Mladic is the commander of the Main Staff which is the corps of the army. They both own it militarily. They both are responsible for it. Mr. Ivetic also -- well, and -- for Butler's words on that topic, you can see transcript 16158 to 16160. Mr. Ivetic also makes the argument that Mladic's Directive 7.1, which comes out March 31st, shortly after Directive 7, somehow replaces the criminal language of Directive 7. This is just not correct. It's clear when you look at the documents side by side, Directive 7.1 cites Directive 7. And Directive 7.1 is very specific and it involves combat operations not involving the enclaves, and it doesn't suggest anything significant about the enclaves. The wording in Directive 7 remains valid and important. We know this because General Zivanovic in Exhibit P1468, sent out on March 20th, before Directive 7.1, I'll tell you, but he cites to Directive 7 in the same exact language to the Drina Corps, the illegal language. But very importantly, on July 2nd the Drina Corps develops Exhibit P1465, it's the Krivaja 95 attack plan. And it's one of the first things you'll see in that attack plan is the citation to Directive 7 and Directive 7.1. They are looked at together. Just as valid at that point. We also, if you'll recall from Krivaja 95 attack plan, Mladic approved it. A copy of that went to the Main Staff and remember the -- there is a map that goes with it, Exhibit P1084. Mladic signed it, made a comment on it. That's his approval of that plan. And in that plan you'll remember the famous language: Reduce the enclave to its urban areas, this small area of 1 by 2 kilometres, that 35.000 people will be jammed into if it's reduced. And also the language: Create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves. This is a reflection of the wording of Directive 7. It's approved by Mladic, developed by the Drina Corps. Mr. Ivetic also argued that the MUP forces in Srebrenica that after the initial combat were acting on their own, not under the command of army -- the army or Mladic. Butler evaluates the key documents on this point from transcript 16206 to 16209. But that first exhibit that Mr. Butler talks about is P2103. You may recall the 10 July order, by then the acting minister, Tomo Kovac, that is an order from Borovcanin to report from the Trnovo front where he is with several units of the special police and other units, and he's to go to the Srebrenica area and report to General Krstic. And Mr. Butler discussed that -- what that language to go to General Krstic meant. That meant, in Butler's view, that he was now under the command of the army. Mr. Butler also in his testimony and in his report refers us to Exhibit P2104, it's Article 14, the law, and entitled: "Use of Police Units in Combat Operations, dated November 29th, 1994." And this describes that when the MUP and the army are working in combat together that the army is in command and that the MUP retains their unit commander like Borovcanin but the army is overall in command. And Kovac's letter is consistent with that law. And Butler speaks to that at 16210 of the transcript. Also to finish this subject, look at Exhibit P724. This is Borovcanin, the commander of the special police forces. This is what we refer to as his after-action report. It's a detailed description of his unit's actions and movements from 11 July to about 20 July. And one of the first things he notes in it is that he reports to Pribicevac, the forward command post, as you recall is just south of Srebrenica, south of Bratunac. And he finds Mladic there and reports to Mladic and receives orders from Mladic to go attack Potocari. This, of course, is an indication that Boro is now under the command, Borovcanin is now under the command of General Mladic in the VRS. You may recall that report and Butler's discussion of it but the -- his forces have not arrived yet, and so he is unable to attack Potocari that night but does attack it the next morning, the 12th of July, takes up position around the enclave, around Potocari, and receives more orders from General Mladic on the 12th of July, personally to go along the road, the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, to set up blockade for the fleeing Muslims where he is on the 13th and 14th, still obviously under the command of General Mladic. Mladic is giving him orders under his own report. So that is very clear. The special police and the units that are working hard in Potocari separating people and working hard along the road capturing people are all under the command of General Mladic. Mr. Ivetic also suggested that General Mladic was not involved in or didn't know anything about the Skorpions and their activities in Trnovo when they butchered six men on video. Now, let's not forget who those men were, and boys. These were people that were last seen in the Srebrenica area. These weren't Sarajevo kids or men. They were reported missing by their family and friends from the enclave when it fell. We put two witnesses on: 92 bis RM311, she ID'd her brother on the tape; RM347, his brother-in-law fled with him in the woods and he didn't see him again. Erin Gallagher told us the names of those six people on the tape and how they were identified by the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, since you were interrupted anyhow, I understood Mr. Ivetic to emphasise that on the side of the perpetrators of those killings, the link was missing with the accused. Now, when you said Mr. Ivetic also suggested that General Mladic was not involved in or didn't know anything about the Skorpions and their activities in Trnovo when they butchered six men on video, you said: "Now, let's not forget who those men were." It seems that you're focusing on the victims and that Mr. Ivetic is focusing on the perpetrators of what is seen on the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm getting to part two of that, to respond specifically to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I never heard Mr. Ivetic say anything that these victims did not come from Srebrenica. So let's try to focus exactly, and I said this earlier to Mr. Traldi, let's try to focus exactly on where the disagreement is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The important point there, Your Honour, is that he's trying to separate General Mladic and the VRS from this killing completely. And my point is that this killing is part of the organised murder operation that was developed by Mladic as you've seen it from the evidence. And so that's the first thing that we need to understand. Mladic cannot escape organised executions of Srebrenica people during this time-period. But that's point one. Point two is that Mr. Ivetic suggested that the Skorpion unit was only working in a co-ordinated action with the VRS. In fact, he said on page 49, 8 through 10, and I quote: "The Skorpion unit itself was operating in co-ordinated action as described by Mr. Theunens rather than being resubordinated to the VRS. This is at transcript page 18715 through 18717," of Mr. Ivetic. Actually, the transcript cited by Mr. Ivetic is from the testimony not of Theunens but of a protected witness, RM280, who did say the Skorpions were working in co-ordination with the VRS. He's a low-level person. What Theunens actually testified to was the Skorpions were subordinated to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and that's at transcript page 20671.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Citing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Citing an Exhibit P3096, which you may recall is a Sarajevo Romanija Corps daily combat report of 23 July, where its commander, Dragomir Milosevic, refers to the Skorpions twice and both times under the heading or in reference to "our forces." utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel. I'll be addressing Counts 1 and 2, genocide; and Counts 9 and 10, terror and unlawful acts on civilians. First, I'll address the arguments made yesterday which were limited to the neighbourhood of Sirokaca. This was part of the 28 May 1992 city-wide shelling described in Scheduled incident G1. You've heard that the entire city of Sarajevo was shelled on this date and that the G1 scheduled incident was not limited to one particular neighbourhood. This attack occurred within the context of the campaign against Sarajevo as set forth in Counts 9 and 10. Between May 1992 and November 1995, General Mladic and his fellow JCE members implemented a campaign of sniping and shelling on Sarajevo. The primary purpose was to spread terror among the civilian population in Sarajevo. The campaign of terror in Sarajevo was a means for members of the Bosnian Serb military and political leadership to achieve their territorial aims. The impact of this campaign was devastating for the people of Sarajevo, where the civilian population lived in a constant state of fear. "Terror" is a term numerous witnesses use to describe the psychological impact this prolonged VRS campaign had on the city. General Mladic played a key role in the implementation of this campaign by commanding the SRK and its tactics of shelling and sniping activities at Sarajevo. This is evident as it pertains to G1 in an intercept, P327, dated 25 May, 1992. We heard General Mladic warn a subordinate to make sure that the soldiers become aware that "Sarajevo is going to shake. Sarajevo will shake, more shells will fall on per second than in the entire war so far." Three days later, on the evening of 28 May 1992, General Mladic issued orders to indiscriminately bombard Sarajevo. Your Honours have heard the recording admitted as Exhibit P105. In this recording, General Mladic instructs a subordinate to fire on the neighbourhoods of the old town and of Pofalici because there weren't many Serbian inhabitants there. During the same conversation, General Mladic said he intended to shell the city so "we drive them out of their minds." In fact, the entire city of Sarajevo was shelled on 28 May 1992, under General Mladic's orders. Several eye-witnesses testified about this incident, including RM115, RM147, John Wilson. RM115 heard General Mladic on the radio ordering the shelling of Sarajevo on the night of 28 May 1995. Hours later, she was hit by a shell that fell on the state hospital in the centre of Sarajevo. I refer Your Honours to P549, pages 71 and 72, which is the Stari Grad log-book which confirms there were victims of shelling, injured and killed, in other parts of Sarajevo. Against this overwhelming evidence, the Defence refers only to the origin of one shell in one neighbourhood. In relation to the evidence of Fadila Tarcin, the Prosecution submits that the information regarding the origin of fire is solely based on hearsay evidence of the witness's neighbours. I would refer you to the transcript of her testimony at 3424, lines 11 through 15. Reviewing the evidence more completely, UNPROFOR's chief military observer, General John Wilson, testified: "It appeared the whole city was being engaged, not just particular areas, but there was an emphasis of fire down in the old city." General Wilson also explained that it was a really horrendous experience for the inhabitants of Sarajevo on that particular night. General Wilson described exactly what General Mladic ordered. Shellings like this set the tone for years to come, and the evidence shows that over three years the actions of General Mladic and the SRK were intentionally designed the terrorise the city's residents. The Prosecution has proven Counts 9 and 10. Your Honours, I'll now address Counts 1 and 2, genocide. In 1992, Bosnian Muslim and Croat communities in the municipalities of Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Kotor Varos, Vlasenica, and Foca were targeted for destruction. Thousands in these communities were killed, subjected to serious bodily and mental harm, and detained in conditions of life which were calculated to destroy them. Those that survived and others were forcibly displaced. In 1995 in Srebrenica, over 7,000 Muslim men and boys were executed while thousands more were forced from the enclave. In the municipalities and in Srebrenica, the combination of physically destructive acts and other acts targeting the foundation of the group such as displacements, the destruction of property, cultural and religious sites, led to the physical demise of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat communities and their inability to reconstitute themselves. Despite these well-established facts, the Defence argues that genocide was not committed and that his client lacked genocidal intent. This approach ignores the facts and the accurate state of law, most recently set forth in the Appeals Chamber 98 bis judgement in the Karadzic case. Let's first turn to a number of the arguments which can be dealt with quickly. First, the ICJ judgement. As Your Honour, Mr. President, noted on the record, at T1615: "I think clear to everyone that the International Court of Justice does not express itself on the individual criminal responsibility of persons but of states." The ICJ reached this determination based on different evidence in applying a different legal standard. It is simply not relevant to your determination here at the 98 bis proceeding. Likewise, the point regarding previous ICTY cases ignores that the genocide count, for the municipalities, have been upheld at the 98 bis stage in all prior cases, whether by the Trial Chamber or the Appeals Chamber following an appeal. Jelesic was acquitted at the trial level, but the Defence yesterday failed to recognise that the Appeals Chamber held that the Trial Chamber erred in doing so and found that the evidence presented supported a finding of genocidal intent. In terms of the Defence urging a review of societal context, this is a misconception of the legal requirements. This is the notion that to prove genocide we must be able to look objectively at a particular scenario on the ground and affix the label "genocide" in isolation from an accused. This is contrary to the legal requirements of the crime of genocide. As to the intent of physical perpetrators, it is not necessary for JCE liability to show that physical perpetrators were acting with genocidal intent. Rather, that their acts are attributable to Mladic through the JCE and that Mladic and other JCE members were acting with genocidal intent. I refer you to the Brdjanin appeals judgement, paragraph 410, and also the Krajisnik appeals judgement, paragraph 226. Finally, the Defence argument for a numerical threshold ignores the legal requirements. It is not necessary to prove that the underlying acts of genocide, in fact, have an impact on the existence of a group, and there is no numerical threshold of victims necessary to establish genocide. It also ignores the fact that for the municipality evidence there are two other major categories of acts of genocide besides killings. For Srebrenica there is one other act of genocide aside from killings. These aren't really arguments. Rather, these are attempts to distract from the voices and images of genocide which have been proven in your presence. The Appeals Chamber judgement on the Karadzic 98 bis genocide charge confirms that at the 98 bis stage the analysis is quite simple: First, that there is evidence that acts of genocide were committed and attributable to Mladic; second, there is evidence that Mladic had genocidal intent with respect to these acts. To further explain, I will first briefly set out the acts of genocide that characterise both genocides in the municipalities and in Srebrenica, and then discuss the mens rea of the JCE members, particularly Mladic and Karadzic. Turning to the 1992 genocide. Consider the detailed evidence presented earlier by Mr. Traldi as the backdrop for the discussion of acts of genocide. Looking specifically at acts of genocide: First, thousands of targeted people were murdered in the six municipalities. Community leaders were often singled out for particularly sadistic violence and were often beaten to death or killed outright. As Adil Medic testified, the Serbs removed those people who represented security for these communities. And that's at transcript page 2050, starting at line 21, and it goes to page 2051, at line 14. Second, serious bodily and mental harm lingers today and indelibly imprints those who survived the brutality. Look at Ivo Atlija's evidence. He survived the murders at Brisevo and spoke bravely here about the murder of his own father and of his neighbours, many of whom he had to bury himself. But he would not name the women in his village who had been sexually assaulted. Because they were so traumatised it was difficult to stop them from killing themselves. And that's at transcript page 2315. In this vein, consider the testimony of RM70, at transcript 17652, lines 12 to 15: "My opinion was that they wanted to destroy, kill, destroy our spirit as much as they could because a raped woman -- there is no cure for a woman who was raped. I will not recover." And third, members of the VRS and other Bosnian Serb forces created conditions of life calculated to destroy thousands more targeted people in the detention camps. You've heard repeatedly that the camps, designed mostly for civilians, were not fit for human habitation. You can look to RM008, who described over 500 detainees crammed into room 3 at Keraterm, and RM088 who pointed out the hangar in P526 in which 600 detainees were jammed. Witness after witness at camp after camp described beatings, torture, sexual violence, and the lack of basic sanitation, depravation of food, water, and medical care. Consistent with Adil Medic's evidence, Your Honours heard that specific prisoners were particularly targeted for abuse and violence. For instance, an Omarska guard told Kerim Mesanovic that he had been put on a "cooling list" to be killed because in the first category of prisoners. Mesanovic explained that this was meant for leaders, intellectuals, and wealthier people. That was at P3414, paragraphs 40 to 42. By the end of 1992, targeted civilians had effectively been driven out of the Serb lands or were forced in enclaves. As a result, the enclaves were bursting with Muslim detainees. By 1995, over 30.000 Muslims were inside the Srebrenica enclave. The existence of the enclaves within Bosnian Serb territories was a point of frustration to Mladic. After initial plans in March of 1995, the attack on Srebrenica began on 6 July 1995, and by the time it was over more than 7.000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were dead and over 30.000 women and children had been forced out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You talked about bursting with Muslim detainees. Did you intend to say that being in the enclave would create a situation of imprisonment or?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I misspoke. What I meant to say was that the enclaves were bursting with Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The discriminatory systemic violence levied across Bosnia in 1992 was applied in Srebrenica in 1995. This violence assured that the objective of the overarching JCE - the destruction of Muslim and Croat communities in Serb claimed Bosnia - was achieved in Srebrenica as it had been in the targeted areas through Bosnia. The Defence claims the Prosecution has not presented sufficient evidence of their client's genocidal intent to pass the 98 bis stage. This is a revisionist view of the trial record. Both direct and indirect evidence provide a sufficient basis for a reasonable chamber to conclude that the accused and other JCE members intended to physically destroy the groups. The direct evidence of the accused's statements alone, taken at its highest, is sufficient to show that the accused had genocidal intent. Mladic's intent was set forth clearly in a number of documents, interviews, and intercepts. Ratko Mladic stated his intent with respect to Bosnian Muslims in 1994 at the 37th Assembly session. He spoke of an objective that the Karadzic Appeals Chamber has considered an indication of genocidal intent. He said: "My concern is not that they will create a state. My concern is to have them vanish completely." P3076, at page 49. Mladic repeatedly made similar comments about Bosnian Muslim and Croat communities in the holdout enclaves. At the most basic and pervasive level, Mladic brought and endorsed a lexicon of derogatory terms and eliminationist rhetoric when referring to the targeted peoples in Bosnia. This sanctioned verbal abuse was widespread, extending into official VRS directives. You can look at P1963. His use of the terms "Ustasha" and "Turks" was directed at enemy forces but also civilians. See at P1969. It is well-established that the use of verbal abuse relating to targeted ethnic groups is a relevant factor in finding genocidal intent. Ratko Mladic's use of these terms reverberated throughout the carnage which his forces imposed on Bosnian Muslim and Croat communities.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. While these direct manifestations of intent alone would be sufficient to find the requisite intent, considerably more evidence is found in Ratko Mladic's conduct. My colleagues have set out in compelling detail for you exactly how forces under Mladic and Karadzic's control turn their genocidal intent into reality and made those targeted populations vanish. The record also reflects the shared genocidal intent of other members of the JCE, in particular the man who selected Mladic to command the military forces, Radovan Karadzic. Karadzic expressed his genocidal intent towards Bosnian Muslims as early as October 1991 when he warned Bosnian Muslims that Bosnian independence would entail "the same highway of hell and suffering" that Slovenia and Croatia went through. He also indicated that this would result "in a possible extinction" of the Muslim people. You'll find this at P2004 at the bottom of page 3 in English, or the transcript reference 15521, lines 16 to 21. As the attacks were well underway in the municipalities, Radovan Karadzic gave the 17th Assembly session, which started on the 24th of July, 1992, an accurate status of the Bosnian Muslim populations: "They think they are being nationally established, but in fact they are vanishing." From P4581, page 86 in the English translation. Karadzic also acknowledged to his followers and subordinates that the groups were being physically destroyed and agreed with the assertion that the conflict had been "roused in order to eliminate the Muslims." That's Exhibit 4581, again at page 86. Beyond the direct evidence of intent, additional evidence considered in totality supports the conclusion that Ratko Mladic and other JCE members had genocidal intent. Genocidal intent can be readily inferred from the scale and repetitiveness of the genocide and other culpable acts in the municipalities, the level of brutality, methods employed, and animus exhibited during the commission of those acts, and the fact that they were all directed against all members of the groups. Genocidal and other culpable acts were directed against and impacted virtually all members of the groups in the municipalities. Your Honours, the first witness in this trial spoke to you as a man, but he portrayed vividly the 13-year-old boy who experienced persecution at its worst. In boyish terms, he described an idyllic rural childhood in a multi-ethnic area in which children played without regard to religion or ethnicity. He and his family were forced from their home. Elvedin described a boy's excitement several days later about returning home and then the heartbreak of finding his home damaged, the mosque destroyed, the elderly left behind murdered, and his dog, whom he was anxious to reunite with, shot dead. Elvedin Pasic and his family fled from village to village and finally into an enclave, from which he and mostly men tried to flee in a column. Surrendering for this group that he was with was not enough. Elvedin lay in the mud and heard his father and other men beaten and abused.
